belief: I have committed the unpardonable sin.
meta: A Christian look at the false belief that you have committed the unpardonable sin, with Scripture, questions, and homework for replacing it with the truth.
origins: A frightening sermon about blasphemy against the Spirit. A blasphemous or angry thought that popped into your mind and would not go away. Saying something against God in a moment of pain. A sensitive or anxious conscience that keeps checking whether you are forgiven. Intrusive, unwanted thoughts are common, especially during anxiety, and they are not the same as a settled choice of the heart.
teaches: Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Spirit to religious leaders who saw His work and deliberately called the Spirit’s work evil. It describes a hardened heart that rejects Christ to the end, not an unwanted thought or a moment of anger. Jesus promised that all other sins and blasphemies can be forgiven. The very fact that you are worried about this, and want God, is strong evidence that your heart is not hardened against Him.
self_statements: I’ve gone too far and God can never forgive me.
That thought proves I blasphemed the Spirit.
I keep checking, and I still don’t feel forgiven.
God has turned His back on me forever.
There’s no point in praying anymore.
errors: Concluding “I feel unforgiven, so I must be unforgivable.”
Treating an unwanted thought as if it were a deliberate act of the heart.
Jumping to the worst possible spiritual conclusion from one moment.
Applying Jesus’ warning to the Pharisees to a frightened believer who wants God.
Ignoring Jesus’ promise that He will never drive away anyone who comes to Him.
questions: Who was Jesus speaking to in Mark 3, and what were they doing?
Do I want to be close to God? Does a hardened heart want that?
Was my thought something I chose and treasure, or something I hate?
What does Jesus say about everyone who comes to Him?
Has my fear grown out of Scripture, or out of anxiety and checking?
If I confess my sins, what does 1 John 1:9 promise?
Would someone who truly rejected the Spirit be this troubled about it?
truth: I have not committed the unpardonable sin. Jesus warned hardened leaders who called His Spirit’s work evil, not frightened believers with unwanted thoughts. My concern about this shows my heart still wants God. Jesus will never drive away anyone who comes to Him, and when I confess, He is faithful to forgive me.
hw_questions: Who was Jesus speaking to, and what were they doing?
Does a hardened heart want to be close to God?
Did I choose this thought, or do I hate it?
What does Jesus promise to all who come to Him?
Is this fear from Scripture or from anxiety?
hw_truths: My worry shows my heart still wants God.
An unwanted thought is not a hardened heart.
Jesus will never drive away anyone who comes to Him.
When I confess, God is faithful to forgive me.
Nothing can separate me from the love of God in Christ.
I do not have to keep checking; I can rest in His promise.
log: Each time I feel the urge to re-check whether I am forgiven, write a mark and read John 6:37 once, instead of reviewing my thoughts.
name_example: Everyone the Father gives Me will come to Me, and when Sarah comes to Me I will never drive her away.
actions: and write who Jesus was speaking to and what they had said about Him.
When the frightening thought comes, let it pass
without arguing with it, praying about it again, or asking for reassurance. Notice what happens to the anxiety.
when you want to ask someone if you are forgiven, wait thirty minutes first, then see if you still need to.
Talk with a pastor or Christian counselor
about intrusive thoughts. Many believers experience them.
tracker: One time I let the thought pass
prayer: Father, thank You that Jesus will never drive away anyone who comes to Him. Help me reject the lie that I have committed the unpardonable sin. Quiet my anxious thoughts, and help me rest in Your promise instead of checking again and again. I come to You, and I trust that You receive me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
songs: Christ bears the burden of rescue rather than demanding self-salvation.
Christ’s sacrifice answers guilt and the effort to pay for one’s own sins.
Grace offers a new beginning rather than defining a person by failure.
Larry Ford and Lillie Knauls with Gaither
